candidate.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity → Coping/Support Systems/Therapeutic Communication: assess psychosocial adaptation to chronic illness and treatment, identify effects on relationships and roles, and coordinate appropriate psychosocial support.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — multidimensional quality-of-life assessment in chronic dialysis
candidate.educational_objective: Include physical, emotional, social, role-function, and treatment-burden effects in ongoing dialysis quality-of-life assessment and communicate these findings to the interdisciplinary team for individualized care planning.

options.A: Assess how kidney failure and dialysis are affecting physical functioning, emotional well-being, relationships, daily roles, and treatment burden, and communicate these findings to the interdisciplinary team for an individualized plan of care.
options.B: Focus only on laboratory targets because psychosocial and quality-of-life concerns do not need to be incorporated into the dialysis plan if dialysis adequacy measures are acceptable.
options.C: Use one identical quality-of-life response plan for every dialysis client because individual social roles, emotional needs, and treatment burden do not change care planning.
options.D: Delay psychosocial assessment until the client requests treatment withdrawal because routine dialysis care addresses physical treatment needs only.

candidate.rationale: CMS requires an individualized comprehensive plan of care for dialysis clients based on the interdisciplinary assessment and changes in the client's condition. The plan must address psychosocial status, including monitoring and social-work interventions, using a standardized mental and physical assessment tool selected by the social worker at regular intervals or more often when needed. Current National Kidney Foundation guidance also recognizes that dialysis can affect physical health, mood, relationships, independence, daily functioning, and overall quality of life. Therefore, A is correct. B excludes required psychosocial care, C conflicts with individualized care planning, and D delays assessment until severe distress or treatment-withdrawal consideration.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports individualized psychosocial and mental/physical quality-of-life assessment as part of the dialysis plan of care rather than limiting care to laboratory or physical-treatment measures.
candidate.source_document_title: ESRD Clinic Services — Patient Plan of Care; Depression and Dialysis
candidate.source_locator: CMS 'ESRD Clinic Services' → Patient POC: the interdisciplinary team must develop an individualized comprehensive plan based on assessment and changes in condition. POC Development → Psychosocial status: necessary monitoring and social-work interventions, including counseling/referrals, measured by a standardized mental and physical assessment tool chosen by the social worker at regular intervals or as needed; rehabilitation status should support the level of productive activity desired by the patient. NKF 'Depression and Dialysis' → dialysis-related depression can affect physical health, relationships, daily functioning, treatment adherence, independence, and quality of life.
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS); National Kidney Foundation
candidate.source_version_date: CMS ESRD Clinic Services current 2026; NKF Depression and Dialysis last updated 2025-08-13
candidate.stem: A client receiving chronic dialysis says, "My laboratory results look acceptable, but dialysis has disrupted my work, relationships, sleep, and mood." Which nursing response best reflects comprehensive dialysis care?
